final_text:
I can't identify the organism that caused the sepsis from this report alone.

**Top non-human species, ranked by clade reads (500,000 total):**

| Species | Clade reads | % of reads | Genus on contaminant list? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cutibacterium acnes | 524 | 0.10% | Not by this name (see below) |
| Acidovorax sp. JMULE5 | 331 | 0.07% | **Yes (acidovorax)** |
| Staphylococcus epidermidis | 182 | 0.04% | No |

**Why the report can't answer the question:**
- **The top species are poor causal candidates.** Acidovorax is a known reagent contaminant. C. acnes and S. epidermidis live on skin and often contaminate blood samples. Each makes up 0.1% of reads or less.
- **C. acnes may also be a contaminant.** Its genus, Cutibacterium, isn't on the list under that name. But the list includes *propionibacterium*, which is the former name of this genus. I didn't flag it, because I applied the list exactly as written.
- **The strongest signal can't be pinned to a species.** 44,055 reads (8.8%) are assigned to the family Enterobacteriaceae (gut bacteria such as E. coli and Klebsiella). Kraken2 couldn't resolve them to a genus or species. Only 154 reads reach E. coli and a handful reach Citrobacter or Klebsiella, so the report doesn't say which member of that family it is.
- **Nothing else is available to settle it.** There is no negative (blank) control to subtract background contamination, and no lab confirmation such as a blood culture.
